sm: James Lindsey opens a short episode about the information environment, with the message to trust but verify. He talks about open source intelligence, or OSINT, where people scour public sources to track money, associations and who works with whom, and he says nearly everyone engaged in online political discourse does some version of it. He lists four problems: the people doing it are mostly amateurs who make mistakes, nothing holds them accountable, they depend on sources they cannot identify, and they may themselves be using pseudonyms or even real looking names, so you may not know who you are listening to. He warns that fake OSINT figures can use limited hangouts and breadcrumb tactics, mixing true things with false ones to lead people astray. He adds that this breeds a distrustful, sectarian and toxic environment, and that even one or two embedded bad actors can damage a network of honest people.

Lindsey says the most dangerous problem is fake sources feeding real OSINT researchers who do not know the sources are fake. He says he cannot vet everyone who sends him messages, that trusted contacts have given him mistakes that embarrassed him, and that he has suspected he was fed bad information. A researcher might have hundreds of sources, and one bad actor among them could build trust with a run of true tips before slipping in something false that leads to a limited hangout. He compares the mechanism to how Tucker Carlson won trust by covering stories others ignored and is now, in Lindsey's view, exploiting that trust to tell lies. Lindsey says he mostly sticks to ideology and primary sources, but everyone, including his audience, must treat open source intelligence with a grain of salt, because the chain of sources can run several steps upstream. He closes by repeating that you have to trust, but verify.
